title: Owned and rented equipment in one view
summary: How digital integration helps United Rentals' field and office teams access key equipment data all in one place
body_markdown:
Rented and owned equipment usually live in different systems, so finding out what is on site, what is idle, and what is still on a truck means checking more than one place.


In a session at[Groundbreak 2026](https://www.procore.com/blog/groundbreak-2026-putting-the-future-of-construction-to-work) , Kris Lengieza, Field COO at Procore, and Tony Leopold, Chief Technology and Strategy Officer of United Rentals, explained how their companies' integration puts rental data in Procore, where field and office teams already work.


### **Key takeaways**


-


**Look at your fleet as one.** Owned and rented equipment in one view makes it easier to decide what to rent, what to move, and what to send back.


-


**Use usage data to find waste.** Alerts and utilization reports on rented units can surface machines that sit idle while the meter runs.


-


**Plan equipment with the schedule.** Last-minute requests raise risk for you and for the rental branch.


-


**Start with what you already use.** Kris said the savings come from using the integration across two products teams already work in every day.


### **When the machine is not there, the work stops**


Tony said rental typically makes up about 2 to 3 percent of project value, but a missing machine pushes crews behind and creates schedule costs that run much higher. He framed the job as three things that have to come together: labor, materials, and equipment.


> "To get the work done, three things have to come together: labor, materials, and equipment. If one is missing, the work doesn’t happen. For United Rentals, it comes down to trust: **customers need to know the equipment will be there when they need it** ."
>
>
> – Tony Leopold, United Rentals


**Learn more about unified resource management** :[Bringing people, equipment, and materials under one roof](https://www.procore.com/blog/unified-resource-management)


### **Equipment planning is the tail on the dog**


Tony said about 58 percent of United Rentals' reservations are for equipment needed today or tomorrow. Some are real emergencies, and some are a forgotten call.


The shorter the lead time, the more risk of a late delivery or a unit in rough condition. He sees the opportunity in tying equipment planning to the schedule data already in Procore.


"Equipment planning is often the tail on the dog. There can be great planning around labor, while rental equipment gets taken for granted," Tony said.


"About 58% of our reservations are for equipment needed today or tomorrow," Tony explained. "Sometimes that’s a genuine emergency, but sometimes it’s simply because nobody planned ahead."


"That’s the opportunity with Procore: Bring equipment into the planning process earlier and reduce that friction."


### **Catch idle rentals before the invoice does**


Telematics shows hourly usage, so teams can flag units that have not run in days or weeks, set alerts, and run utilization reports. Tony described walking in, seeing a dashboard with seven units to check, and asking the trade whether they still need them.


"Telematics shows you how much each piece of equipment is actually being used, so it’s easy to flag something that hasn’t run in three, seven, or 28 days," Tony said. "That lets you identify equipment you’re paying for but may no longer need. Through Procore, we can put that visibility directly into the customer’s workflow, making it easy to see what needs attention and take action."


**Learn more about managing equipment** :[Eliminating equipment blind spots with integrated telematics](https://www.procore.com/blog/equipment-blind-spots-telematics)


### **Automation on a bad process is just a faster bad process**


Asked about autonomous equipment and robotics, Tony expects adoption to take time, with real penetration in about ten years. Kris pointed to his own move from chalk lines to robotic total stations: the setup changes how the work gets done, so teams should look at the whole process, not just the tool.


"I think there's a lot of similarities between what's happening with AI, and I'll call it, digital automation versus physical automation as well," said Kris. "They take a lot of change management, getting people to think about things differently. If you have a bad process and you put automation on top of it, just a faster bad process, you know?"
